title: Influence Doesn’t Come With The Title
author: Andrea Chiarelli et al.
source: The Art of Asking Questions (theartofaskingquestions.com), November 15, 2026
summary: Andrea Chiarelli and co-authors argue that influence is not a personality trait but a cluster of distinct, practicable capabilities. Drawing on Gerald Ferris's Political Skill Inventory, they show that political skill barely correlates with general ability and only modestly with extraversion, and that skilled influencers inspire trust because their attention points outward at the people in the room. They describe influence as three layers: capabilities (social astuteness, interpersonal flexibility, networking and apparent sincerity), situational knowledge of what each party wants and what you can offer, and beliefs that cap what you are willing to try. They then offer four steps for the week: identify your growth edge, break down one live situation, start with the easiest experiment, and let small wins compound. The post ends by introducing a paid AI coaching tool that walks readers through the same process.
points: Political skill is largely independent of intelligence and only modestly tied to extraversion, so influence is learnable rather than innate.
Influence has three layers, capabilities, situational knowledge and beliefs, and any one of them can be the bottleneck.
Apparent sincerity is the enabler of the other capabilities, since the same moves read as manipulative or trustworthy depending on how they are done.
A situational analysis of desired outcome, decision-makers, their priorities and your leverage turns vague advice into a next step.
Starting with a small low-stakes experiment, such as asking a stakeholder what they are weighing, tests limiting beliefs and builds relational capital that compounds.
quotes: Organisations are political systems, in the sense that outcomes get shaped by relationships as much as by evidence, and competence on its own has never been enough to move them.

Influence is not a personality trait: Part of the reason why this is so difficult is that influence gets treated as a mysterious quality that people either have or lack, whereas the research describes something a lot more specific.

Second, people who score highly on political skill aren’t described as more assertive or self-promoting, but as inspiring trust. They have a self-assurance that doesn’t read as arrogant, which makes sense once you notice their attention is pointed outward, at the meeting and the people in it, rather than inward at how they’re coming across. What observers interpret as confidence is often just attention aimed somewhere useful.

Neither approach is the grown-up version of the other, and neither predicts on its own how influential you’ll be. What matters is whether you can change your strategy depending on who you are talking to.
This is not charm in the abstract. It’s a list of people who already trust you because you built a relationship over time, when nothing was at stake.
Quite commonly, people fail to ask what the other party wants, which should actually be the starting point.
Plenty of people know the theory perfectly well and still avoid hard conversations, or arrange things so they get the result they always get.
Influence built this way is not one dramatic moment, but it’s harder to lose, since it rests on accumulated capabilities and relational capital.
context: The opening claim is that organisations run on relationships as well as evidence, so competence alone stalls.
Reframing influence as specific skills rather than a trait is what makes it something a person can work on.
Research on political skill shows trust comes from outward attention, not from self-promotion.
Adaptability to the individual, not a fixed style, is what the research links to effectiveness.
Networking is described as trust built in advance, not charm applied when a favour is needed.
A common failure is never asking what the other party wants, which should be the starting point.
Limiting beliefs explain why knowing the theory still fails to change behaviour.
The closing logic is that small repeated interactions build standing that is durable and hard to lose.
